questions.question: What is X25519 primarily used for in real protocols?
options: Key agreement (ECDH) to derive a shared secret
Digital signatures for message authenticity
Hashing messages into fixed-size digests
Encrypting data directly without a KDF
questions.explanation: X25519 is a scalar-multiplication function used for ECDH-style key agreement; you feed its output into a KDF.

questions.question: In X25519, what do the 32-byte inputs represent?
options: A scalar (private key bytes) and a u-coordinate (public key bytes), both little-endian
Two independent AES keys used for encryption and MAC
A nonce and a ciphertext tag for authenticated encryption
A signature (R,s) split into two 32-byte halves
questions.explanation: X25519 takes 32 scalar bytes and 32 u-coordinate bytes (both little-endian encodings) and outputs a 32-byte u-coordinate.

questions.question: Why does X25519 'clamp' certain bits of the private scalar bytes before scalar multiplication?
options: To force the scalar into a safe form (multiple of the cofactor and within a fixed range)
To make the output u-coordinate look uniformly random without any math assumptions
To ensure the peer’s public key is on the curve by construction
To prevent hash collisions in the protocol transcript
questions.explanation: Clamping sets/clears specific bits so the scalar has a fixed shape, which helps avoid edge cases and improves robustness against certain invalid inputs.

questions.question: What does the Montgomery ladder buy you in X25519 implementations?
options: A regular sequence of operations for all scalars, which helps resist simple side-channel leakage
A way to compute full (x,y) points so you can do signatures directly
A shortcut that avoids modular arithmetic entirely
A guarantee that no invalid public keys can be provided by an attacker
questions.explanation: The ladder performs the same pattern of field operations for each scalar bit, which is a key building block for constant-time implementations.

questions.question: In an ECDH exchange using X25519, what should you do with the raw 32-byte shared secret output before using it as an encryption key?
options: Run it through a KDF (e.g., HKDF) with context (public keys / protocol info)
Use it directly as an AES key with no further processing
Base64-encode it and treat the string as the key material
Hash only the peer public key and ignore the shared secret
questions.explanation: The shared secret is key material, not a ready-to-use session key; a KDF binds context and produces keys of the right length.

questions.question: Attack-themed: RFC 7748 notes that X25519 can output the all-zero value for certain malicious/degenerate public inputs. What is the recommended mitigation in an ECDH protocol?
options: Check for an all-zero shared secret and abort the handshake if it occurs
Ignore it because an all-zero secret is just as secure as any other
Clamp the peer public key bytes the same way as the private scalar
Retry scalar multiplication until the output is non-zero
questions.explanation: An all-zero output can indicate a small-order/invalid input; protocols commonly check for all-zero and abort to avoid key compromise.

questions.question: X25519 treats u-coordinates as little-endian byte strings. What common bug can this cause in implementations?
options: Interpreting inputs as big-endian and deriving incompatible keys
Forgetting to pad AES blocks to 16 bytes
Reusing nonces in AEAD modes by accident
Mixing up RSA public exponent with modulus
questions.explanation: Many crypto APIs use big-endian integers, but X25519 specifies little-endian encodings; endianness mistakes break interoperability.

questions.question: Which statement best describes what X25519 returns?
options: A 32-byte little-endian encoding of the u-coordinate of the scalar-multiplied point
A compressed Edwards point encoding (y plus sign bit)
A pair of coordinates (u,v) that uniquely identifies the curve point
A signature over the transcript that authenticates the exchange
questions.explanation: X25519 outputs only the u-coordinate (x-coordinate in Montgomery form), encoded as 32 bytes little-endian with the top bit cleared.
